question:
Why isn't this emitting the message?

@app.route('/3x3/online/<username>', methods = ['POST']) def online3x3(username): if username == session['username']: socketio.emit('create', (session['username'], 1), namespace = '/3x3/online/{username}') session['ready'] = False Anybody know why this isn't being properly received? I'm very new to Flask, Socketio and Javascript so would appreciate any suggestions, for some reason the javascript code isn't receiving anything
reference_answer: Using dynamic namespaces with Flask-SocketIO is not possible. However, you can use static namespaces and rooms. Based on your example code, it's difficult to understand your requirements. The following simple example demonstrates the use of rooms in the standard namespace. A maximum of two people can meet and send messages in a room. The room name is generated randomly. """ Required package installations: % pip install flask flask-session flask-socketio """ from flask import Flask, render_template, session from flask_session import Session from flask_socketio import SocketIO, join_room, leave_room, emit import random, string app = Flask(__name__) app.config.from_mapping( SECRET_KEY='your secret here', SESSION_TYPE='filesystem' ) socketio = SocketIO(app) rooms = {} def generate_room_code(length, existing_codes): while True: code_chars = random.choices(string.ascii_letters, k=length) code = ''.join(code_chars) if code not in existing_codes: return code @app.route('/') def index(): session.clear() return render_template('index.html') @socketio.on('disconnect') def on_disconnect(): username = session.pop('name') room = session.pop('room') if username is None or room is None: return leave_room(room) rooms[room]['members'] -= 1 if rooms[room]['members'] <= 0: del rooms[room] emit('message', {'msg': f'{username} has left room {room}'}, room=room) @socketio.on('join') def on_join(data): if session.get('room'): return username = data['username'] room = data['roomname'] if not room or room not in rooms or rooms[room]['members'] >= 2: room = generate_room_code(6, list(rooms.keys())) r
llm_attempt: The namespace argument isn't an f-string: namespace='/3x3/online/{username}' is a literal string, so {username} never gets substituted with the actual value - every emit goes to a namespace nobody is ever connected to (clients connect to a concrete path like /3x3/online/alice, not the literal text /3x3/online/{username}). Fix the immediate bug with namespace=f'/3x3/online/{username}'. But per-user dynamic namespaces are an anti-pattern in Flask-SocketIO: namespaces are meant to be a small fixed set the client connects to, not one-per-user. Better: have the client connect to a single namespace, call join_room(session['username']) in your 'connect' handler, and emit with room=username instead of a dynamic namespace. Also double check the JS client is actually connecting to whatever namespace/path you use, and that session['username'] is actually set at the time this route runs (sessions aren't shared between the Socket.IO connection and unrelated HTTP requests unless cookies are configured correctly).

question:
pandas pivot_table: can aggfunc work over a different grouping period from the table?

I have a pandas pivot table that shows payments made to different payees vs date, and I'm using a Grouper to group them into months, e.g.: payee payee_1 payee_2 date 2019-11-30 amount amount 2019-12-31 amount amount 2020-01-31 amount amount 2020-02-29 amount amount I can use the standard aggfunc="sum" to show the "amounts" as the sum for each month, but what I want is to show the sum for 12 months up to each month. Is a custom aggregation function a way to do that? If so, how do I get the values to supply to the function? This is a snippet of raw the data frame: date payee value 0 2020-10-13 payee_1 -43.74 1 2025-01-26 payee_1 -2.03 2 2022-04-08 payee_2 -9.54 3 2021-06-05 payee_1 -16.06 4 2021-12-08 payee_2 -20 And my pivot table definition: pd.pivot_table( df, values="value", index=pd.Grouper( freq="ME", key="date" ), columns="payee", aggfunc="sum", )
reference_answer: You can't reuse the same input data points for different output rows in a pivot_table . What you need is a rolling operation. Since you have a sum, you can perform it after the pivot_table . As months are not valid (non-fixed) frequencies for rolling operations, you would first need to reindex to fill the missing month-ends, then rolling.sum : idx = pd.date_range(*df['date'].agg(['min', 'max']), freq='ME') # DatetimeIndex(['2020-10-31', '2020-11-30', '2020-12-31', ..., # '2024-10-31', '2024-11-30', '2024-12-31'], # dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq='ME') out = ( pd.pivot_table( df, values='value', index=pd.Grouper(freq='ME', key='date'), columns='payee', aggfunc='sum', ) .reindex(idx.rename('date')) .rolling(12, min_periods=1).sum() ) Output: payee payee_1 payee_2 date 2020-10-31 -43.74 NaN 2020-11-30 -43.74 NaN 2020-12-31 -43.74 NaN 2021-01-31 -43.74 NaN 2021-02-28 -43.74 NaN 2021-03-31 -43.74 NaN 2021-04-30 -43.74 NaN 2021-05-31 -43.74 NaN 2021-06-30 -59.80 NaN 2021-07-31 -59.80 NaN 2021-08-31 -59.80 NaN 2021-09-30 -59.80 NaN 2021-10-31 -16.06 NaN 2021-11-30 -16.06 NaN 2021-12-31 -16.06 -20.00 2022-01-31 -16.06 -20.00 2022-02-28 -16.06 -20.00 2022-03-31 -16.06 -20.00 2022-04-30 -16.06 -29.54 2022-05-31 -16.06 -29.54 2022-06-30 NaN -29.54 2022-07-31 NaN -29.54 2022-08-31 NaN -29.54 2022-09-30 NaN -29.54 2022-10-31 NaN -29.54 2022-11-30 NaN -29.54 2022-12-31 NaN -9.54 2023-01-31 NaN -9.54 2023-02-28 NaN -9.54 2023-03-31 NaN -9.54 2023-04-30 NaN NaN 2023-05-31 NaN NaN 2023-06-30 NaN NaN 2023-07-31 NaN NaN 2023-08-31 NaN NaN 2023-09-30 NaN NaN 2023-10-31 NaN NaN 2023-11-30 NaN NaN
llm_attempt: pivot_table's aggfunc only ever sees the values inside one group; it can't reach outside its own bucket to pull in the previous 11 months, so there's no aggfunc trick that does this in a single pivot_table call. The standard approach is two steps: first pivot to one row per month per payee with aggfunc='sum' (what you already have), then apply a trailing 12-month rolling sum on that monthly result: monthly = pd.pivot_table(df, values='value', index=pd.Grouper(freq='ME', key='date'), columns='payee', aggfunc='sum').fillna(0); rolling_12mo = monthly.rolling(window=12, min_periods=1).sum(). Rolling works cleanly here because the pivoted index is already one row per month, sorted chronologically. If you'd rather get NaN than a partial sum for months without 12 full prior periods, use min_periods=12 instead of 1.

question:
What does the uvw command do?

When I install uv though winget, the uv , uvx and uvw aliases get added. I know that uvx is an alias for uv tool run , but what is uvw an alias for?
reference_answer: It's not documented, but uvw is a Windows-specific alias for "uv without a new window". It was proposed in PR #11786 . It's not a bash alias or anything like that, so I don't know if there's an exact translation to an expanded command. However, it internally uses Windows's CREATE_NO_WINDOW flag while spawning the process.
llm_attempt: uvw is the Windows 'windowed' counterpart of uv, analogous to python.exe vs pythonw.exe. It's the same executable as uv but built against the Windows GUI subsystem instead of the console subsystem, so launching it doesn't pop up or attach to a console window. It exists mainly so that installed GUI-script entry points (a tool with gui_scripts, e.g. a Tk/Qt app installed via uv tool install) can be launched through a uv-managed shim without a terminal window flashing up - the same reason pip/distlib ship both console and windowed launcher stubs on Windows. You generally won't invoke uvw directly yourself; it's an implementation detail of how uv creates entry-point shims on Windows, whereas uvx (uv tool run) is the one meant for everyday interactive use.

llm_attempt: Broad question, so here's the general recipe: base your image on an NVIDIA CUDA devel image matching your host driver (e.g. nvidia/cuda:12.2.0-devel-ubuntu22.04), install build tools (build-essential, cmake, python3, python3-pip), then build llama-cpp-python with GPU support baked in via: CMAKE_ARGS='-DGGML_CUDA=on' pip install llama-cpp-python --no-cache-dir --force-reinstall (older versions used LLAMA_CUBLAS=on). question:
What do ** (double star/asterisk) and * (star/asterisk) inside square brakets mean for class and function declarations in Python 3.12+?

What does T, *Ts, **P mean when they are used in square brackets directly after a class or function name or with the type keyword? class ChildClass[T, *Ts, **P]: ... def foo[T, *Ts, **P](arg: T) -> Callable[P, tuple[T, *Ts]]: type vat[T, *Ts, **P] = Callable[P, tuple[T, *Ts]] See complementary questions about ** and * for function parameters and arguments: What do ** (double star/asterisk) and * (star/asterisk) mean in a function call? What does ** (double star/asterisk) and * (star/asterisk) do for parameters?
reference_answer: Python 3.12, in relation to PEP 695 , introduced some grammar changes which bring some features from the typing library into the syntax of the language itself. In short: Each of the 0-to-2-starred expressions T , *Ts , and **P is a type parameter . They are used as a parameters for type parameter lists which can be used for functions, classes and the type statement to create a TypeAliasType . A type parameter list, encapsulated by [] may follow the name of a class, function, or typevar after a type statement and will create a generic . Type-checkers can infer the type of attributes and calls for example: class ClassA[T]: def method1(self) -> T: ... def create[T, *Ts](arg: T, *args: *Ts) -> ClassA[tuple[T, *Ts]]: ... a = create(1, 2, 3) # a inferred as ClassA[tuple[int, int, int]] t = a.method1() # t inferred as tuple[int, int, int] Inside a type parameter list the three different amounts of asterisks have the following meaning: A non-starred identifier, e.g. T is the equivalent to typing.TypeVar and is interpreted as a single type . An identifier prefixed with a single asterisk, e.g. *Ts , is the equivalent to typing.TypeVarTuple and is interpreted as a tuple of types . The single-asterisk prefix * before a TypeVarTuple is equivalent to using typing.Unpack which can be seen similar to a normal unpacking just for types, e.g. tuple[int, *tuple[int, str]] is equivalent to tuple[int, int, str] . Using a TypeVarTuple makes it variable what types are unpacked. Two asterisk before an identifer, e.g. **P , denote a ParamSpec , which in turn stands for the parameters of a callable.
llm_attempt: This is PEP 695 generic syntax (Python 3.12+) combined with PEP 646 and PEP 612. T is an ordinary TypeVar: a single type parameter. *Ts is a TypeVarTuple: it captures an arbitrary-length, ordered sequence of types (like *args does for values), used for variadic generics such as array shapes or heterogeneous tuples - Ts can expand to zero or more types. **P is a ParamSpec: it captures an entire callable's parameter signature (both positional and keyword parameters) as one unit, so you can write higher-order functions/decorators that preserve the exact call signature of a wrapped callable, referencing it via Callable[P, ReturnType] or P.args/P.kwargs. All three replace the pre-3.12 pattern of declaring TypeVar('T'), TypeVarTuple('Ts'), ParamSpec('P') separately and passing them into Generic[...]. type vat[T, *Ts, **P] = ... is a generic type alias using the new 'type' statement, equivalent to the old TypeAlias pattern but with its own scoped type parameters.

Something like: import subprocess import configparser config = configparser.ConfigParser(allow_no_value=True) config.read(r"Settings.ini") videofile = config.get("settings", "videofile") outputfile = config.get("settings", "outputfile") codesplit = config.get("settings", "codesplit", fallback=None) codec = config.get("settings", "codec", fallback=None) ffmpeg_path = r"ffmpeg.exe" command = [ ffmpeg_path, "-i", videofile ] if codesplit: command.append(codesplit) if codec: command.append(codec) command.append(outputfile) # lines commented out for testing # # process = subprocess.Popen( # command, # stdout=subprocess.PIPE, # stderr=subprocess.PIPE, # text=True, # bufsize=1, # universal_newlines=True, # ) # process.communicate() print(command) Using the above Python script I jget the following results from the four sample config.ini files: C:\Users\test>python test.py ['ffmpeg.exe', '-i', 'video.avi', '-vn', 'copy', 'audio.mp3'] C:\Users\test>python test.py ['ffmpeg.exe', '-i', 'video.avi', 'videoaudio.mp4'] C:\Users\test>python test.py ['ffmpeg.exe', '-i', 'video.avi', 'copy', 'videoaudio.mp4'] C:\Users\test>python test.py ['ffmpeg.exe', '-i', 'video.avi', '-vn', 'audio.mp3']
llm_attempt: Your if codesplit and codec / else structure only has two branches, so it can't express 'one present, one missing.' Build the command incrementally instead of branching on both at once: command = [ffmpeg_path, '-i', videofile]; if codesplit: command.append(codesplit); if codec: command.append(codec); command.append(outputfile). Since config.get(..., allow_no_value=True) returns either None (no value at all) or '' (empty string after '='), and both are falsy, 'if codesplit:' and 'if codec:' correctly skip either one independently while keeping the other, giving you all four combinations you listed without nested if/elif logic.

question:
Why do i get "maximum recursion depth exceeded" in my code for the Collatz sequence?

Just started learning Python from Automate the Boring Stuff and would like some clarity about why this specific code I made for Chapter 4 Collatz Sequence doesn't work, but this other code does. I'm having issues understanding how the code is called and why it seems for my code I get an error of maximum recursion depth exceeded. I will post the other code that is correct, so can anyone explain the difference between both codes? Is there any way to modify my code so it works, or do I have to do what the other code says where I need to define the function and the while loop can't be inside the function? Because to me that's what seems like what the issue is. My code: def collatz(number): while number != 1: number=collatz(number) if number % 2 == 0: print ((int(number))//(2),sep='') return ((int(number))//(2)) elif number % 2 == 1: print (3*int(number)+1,sep='') return (3*int(number)+1) print('Enter number:') number=int(input('>')) collatz(number) Correct code: def collatz(number): if number % 2 ==0: #even number print ((int(number))//(2),sep='') return ((int(number))//(2)) elif number % 2 ==1:#odd number print (3*int(number)+1,sep='') return (3*int(number)+1) try: print('Enter number:') number=int(input('>')) #user input while number !=1: #performs loop until number becomes 1 number=collatz(number) #number gets passed to collatz function until it arrives at 1 except ValueError: print('Please enter an integer')#error message if non-integer is input
reference_answer: You are looping all over, you pass the number to the function, number != 1, then call the function with the same number itself, and do not modify it. You need to pass the modified number and call the function again def collatz(number): while number != 1: if number % 2 == 0: print ((int(number))//(2),sep='') return collatz((int(number))//(2)) elif number % 2 == 1: print (3*int(number)+1,sep='') return collatz(3*int(number)+1) return number print('Enter number:') number=35421 collatz(number)
llm_attempt: Your version calls collatz() recursively from inside its own while loop, but the recursive call number=collatz(number) passes the current, unchanged number - the even/odd branch that actually computes the next value never runs before that recursive call happens. So collatz(n) immediately calls collatz(n) again with the same n, which does the same thing, forever: it's unconditional infinite recursion regardless of the input, hence 'maximum recursion depth exceeded.' The 'correct' code avoids this because collatz() is a pure one-step transform with no loop inside it - it computes and returns the next value for a single step, and the while loop lives in the caller, calling collatz() again only after getting the previous result back. Fix your version by removing the while loop from inside the function entirely (one step per call), or alternatively drop the recursive self-call and do the transform directly, driving iteration purely from the outer while loop as the reference code does.

question:
"exclude-newer" does not respect duration

I have a python project with uv where I want to set an exclude-newer policy but it ignores duration. In my pyproject.toml I have [tool.uv] exclude-newer = "7 days" However when I run e.g. uv add [some_package] it gives me a warning: warning: Failed to parse `pyproject.toml` during settings discovery: TOML parse error at line 43, column 17 | 43 | exclude-newer = "7 days" | ^^^^^^^^ failed to parse year in date "7 days": failed to parse "7 da" as year (a four digit integer): invalid digit, expected 0-9 but got uv docs say Accepts RFC 3339 timestamps (e.g., 2006-12-02T02:07:43Z ), a "friendly" duration (e.g., 24 hours , 1 week , 30 days ), or an ISO 8601 duration (e.g., PT24H , P7D , P30D ). I tried setting it to the ISO duration and it gives the same warning. When I set it to a specific datetime it works. How can I set it to work with a duration like a number of days? I have uv 0.9.2 and Python 3.11.14.
reference_answer: Per the 0.9.x changelog , allowing a relative exclude-newer was not added until v0.9.17: 0.9.17 Released on 2025-12-09. Enhancements ... Add support for relative durations in exclude-newer (a.k.a., dependency cooldowns) ( #16814 ) Therefore you will need to upgrade to at least this version (the release reflected in the documentation is v0.11.10 at time of writing).
llm_attempt: This looks like a version gap rather than something you're doing wrong: 'friendly'/ISO-8601 duration parsing for exclude-newer was added to uv at some point, and depending on exactly when that landed relative to 0.9.2, it may not be fully wired up for the [tool.uv] pyproject.toml key yet even though the docs describe it (vs. only the --exclude-newer CLI flag/env var supporting it). First try uv self update to get the latest release and retest - this is exactly the kind of thing that gets fixed between patch versions. If it still fails, search astral-sh/uv's GitHub issues for 'exclude-newer duration pyproject'; a report likely already exists. As a workaround meanwhile, compute an absolute RFC 3339 timestamp for 'now minus 7 days' yourself (e.g. in a small CI script) and set exclude-newer to that literal timestamp instead of a relative duration.

question:
Optional field in Pydantic v2

The following code is expected to fail with bs "Field required". But how can I change class A to make the field bs optional and not just the value of bs ? I'm using v2.11.5. from typing import Optional, TypedDict, List from pydantic import TypeAdapter class B(TypedDict): number: int class A(TypedDict): name: str value: int bs: Optional[List[B]] = None data_with_list = { "name":"alfa", "value":1, "bs" : [ {"number":1001}, {"number":1002} ] } data_with_empty_list = { "name":"beta", "value":2, "bs" : [ {"number":1003}, {"number":1004} ] } data_with_no_list = { "name":"gamma", "value":3, } ta = TypeAdapter(A) ta.validate_python(data_with_list) ta.validate_python(data_with_empty_list) ta.validate_python(data_with_no_list)
reference_answer: That is more about the standard library typing (in particular TypedDict) than pydantic itself. You may want to inherit pydantic's BaseModel and use them as proper models instead, but if you want to keep using TypedDict you have two options. Either you set total=False such that all keys are treated as optional Or you explicitly set the key that may be missing as NotRequired
llm_attempt: TypedDict doesn't support field defaults the way a dataclass or BaseModel does - bs: Optional[List[B]] = None doesn't make the key optional-to-omit, it's ignored for requiredness purposes, which is why bs still comes back as required. To mark a TypedDict key as not required, use NotRequired (PEP 655): from typing import NotRequired; class A(TypedDict): name: str; value: int; bs: NotRequired[Optional[List[B]]]. That makes bs both optional to omit and nullable, so all three of your validate_python calls should pass. question:
Time interval between frames on facial landmarks extraction

I'm used to working with MediaPipe in Python on a Windows 11 desktop setup. In this environment, if VIDEO mode is selected, MediaPipe automatically reads the video frame count, and the detected frames are processed directly. Recently, I started working on an Android implementation of my existing project using MediaPipe. However, I noticed that on Android (specifically for facial landmark extraction ), MediaPipe requires a time interval between frames to be specified. Because of this, I end up with different frame counts and landmark predictions when processing the same video on both devices, even when using the same face_landmarker.task file. Despite this adjustment, I still get different predictions and frame counts . This isn't too surprising, since the FPS value I read isn't that close to a clean integer.
reference_answer: On android the tasks API never reads video properties by itself. You must decode the video externally, decide which frames to feed and provide monotonically increasing timestamps, so you get consistent frame counts and predictions between desktop and Android. Also, make sure both sides are using the same frame sampling strategy. If you still see differences, consider switching both platforms to IMAGE mode and process the exact same set of extracted frames. val presentationTimeUs = bufferInfo.presentationTimeUs val timestampMs = presentationTimeUs / 1000L // MediaPipe expects ms faceLandmarker.detect( mpImage, // your Image built from the decoded frame timestampMs ) This way the timestamps on android match the actual presentation timestamps of the video, which is the closest behavior to python’s video mode. And do let me know how it went for you.
llm_attempt: On Android, the Tasks API's FaceLandmarker VIDEO mode has no built-in video file reader the way your desktop pipeline apparently does - you're expected to decode frames yourself and supply a timestamp for each detectForVideo() call, so there's no setting to turn that requirement off. The frame-count/prediction mismatch is most likely because you're feeding a constant interval derived from a rounded FPS (29 vs 30) rather than each frame's real presentation timestamp. Instead of computing timestamps from an assumed FPS, pull the actual per-frame timestamps from the decoder (e.g. MediaExtractor.getSampleTime() or MediaMetadataRetriever, converted to ms) and pass those exact values to detectForVideo(); that makes both frame count and timing match the container's real structure instead of an approximation, which should bring Android's output much closer to the desktop result. Exact bit-for-bit parity isn't guaranteed since the two paths use different decoders, but matching real timestamps should remove most of the divergence.

question:
How can I efficiently parallelize and optimize a large-scale graph traversal algorithm in Python to handle millions of nodes?

I'm working on Python project that involves processing a very large graph - it has millions of nodes and edges. The goal is to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) or depth-first search (DFS) from a given start node to compute shortest paths or reachability. Here's the challenge : The graph is too large to fit comfortably into memory if stored natively. The traversal needs to be fast, ideally leveraging multiple CPU cores. I want to avoid race conditions and ensure thread-safe updates to shared data structures. The graph data is stored as adjacency lists in files, and I want to process it efficiently without loading the entire graph at once. Currently, I have a basic BFS implementation using a Python dictionary for adjacency, but it runs slowly and hits memory limits: from collections import deque def bfs(graph, start): visited = set() queue = deque([start]) while queue: node = queue.popleft() if node not in visited: visited.add(node) queue.extend(graph.get(node, [])) return visited Question How can I parallelize BFS/DFS in Python to speed up traversal? Should I use multiprocessing , concurrent.features , or another approach? I'm open to suggestions involving alternative algorithms (like bidirectional BFS), external databases, or memory-mapped files. I’ve tried the following: A basic BFS using Python’s built-in set , deque , and dict , as shown in the code. Storing the entire adjacency list in memory using a dictionary of lists, but this doesn’t scale well for millions of nodes. I attempted to use the multiprocessing module to run multiple BFS instances in parallel from dif
llm_attempt: There's no single-snippet fix here - this is a systems-design problem, and plain Python (GIL-bound, dict/set-based) is a poor fit at millions-of-nodes scale regardless of how you parallelize it. Concretely: (1) BFS/DFS parallelizes at the frontier level - expand all nodes in the current frontier concurrently, merge into the next frontier, repeat; this needs process-based parallelism (multiprocessing, not threading, since traversal is CPU/dict-lookup bound), with the visited set partitioned by node-owner or synchronized via shared memory. (2) Rather than hand-rolling this, use a library with a compiled core: graph-tool or igraph for single-machine performance (far faster than networkx, much lower memory via CSR-style storage), or cuGraph if you have a GPU. (3) For out-of-core graphs, store the adjacency list as memory-mapped CSR arrays (numpy memmap) instead of a dict of lists, or push the graph into a database or a GraphFrames/Spark, Pregel-style distributed BFS if it doesn't fit one machine. Bidirectional BFS only helps for single-pair shortest path, not full reachability.

question:
Flatten multindex column in a pipe in pandas

Suppose I have the following DataFrame: arrays = [[1, 1, 2, 2], ["red", "blue", "red", "blue"]] ix = pd.MultiIndex.from_arrays(arrays, names=("number", "color")) df = pd.DataFrame([[10, 20, 30, 40], [50, 60, 70, 80]], columns=ix) df I would like to flatten the MultiIndex column like that: df.columns = [str(x[0])+"_"+str(x[1]) for x in df.columns] df But I would like to do it in a pipe. For instance, supposing the function rename_columns would exist (it doesn't), it would look like: df.rename_columns(lambda x: str(x[0])+"_"+str(x[1])) Said otherwise, I would like to write that rename_columns function. How can I achieve this? The rename function doesn't work: df.rename(lambda x: str(x[0])+"_"+str(x[1])) --------------------------------------------------------------------------- TypeError Traceback (most recent call last) Cell In[28], line 1 ----> 1 df.rename(lambda x: str(x[0])+"_"+str(x[1])) File .venv\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\frame.py:6471, in DataFrame.rename(self, mapper, index, columns, axis, copy, inplace, level, errors) 6352 """ 6353 Rename columns or index labels. 6354 (...) 6468 4 3 6 6469 """ 6470 self._check_copy_deprecation(copy) -> 6471 return super()._rename( 6472 mapper=mapper, 6473 index=index, 6474 columns=columns, 6475 axis=axis, 6476 inplace=inplace, 6477 level=level, 6478 errors=errors, 6479 ) File .venv\Lib\site-packages\pandas\core\generic.py:1065, in NDFrame._rename(self, mapper, index, columns, axis, inplace, level, errors) 1058 missing_labels = [ 1059 label 1060 for index, label in enumerate(replacements) 1061 if indexer[index] == -1 1062 ] 1063
reference_answer: An easy approach would be to use pipe + set_axis : df.pipe( lambda df: df.set_axis( [str(x[0]) + '_' + str(x[1]) for x in df.columns], axis=1 ) ) Output: 1_red 1_blue 2_red 2_blue 0 10 20 30 40 1 50 60 70 80 For a generic approach (independent of the number of levels): def flatten_columns(df, sep='_'): cols = df.columns.to_frame().astype(str).agg(sep.join, axis=1).tolist() return df.set_axis(cols, axis=1) df.pipe(flatten_columns) And even more generic, handling any axis: def flatten_levels(df, sep='_', axis=1): vals = ( df.axes[axis].to_frame().astype(str).agg('_'.join, axis=1).tolist() ) return df.set_axis(vals, axis=axis) df.pipe(flatten_levels) # 1_red 1_blue 2_red 2_blue # lvl0 lvl1 # 1 A 10 20 30 40 # B 50 60 70 80 df.pipe(flatten_levels, axis=0) # number 1 2 # color red blue red blue # 1_A 10 20 30 40 # 1_B 50 60 70 80
llm_attempt: rename(mapper) with a single positional argument and no axis/columns keyword targets the index by default, not columns - that's why it errors: your row index is a plain RangeIndex, so pandas calls your lambda with a bare int, and x[0] on an int raises TypeError. Passing df.rename(columns=lambda x: f'{x[0]}_{x[1]}') instead should target columns properly, but the simplest option guaranteed to work - since it's exactly your already-working non-piped line - is to wrap it in a plain function and use pipe: def flatten_columns(df): df = df.copy(); df.columns = ['_'.join(map(str, c)) for c in df.columns]; return df. Then: df.pipe(flatten_columns). pipe doesn't require a named DataFrame method; any callable taking and returning a DataFrame works, which is exactly how you get your own 'rename_columns'-like chainable step without pandas needing to support it natively.

question:
Floor of Natural Logarithm

I have an arbitrarily large integer n . How would I calculate the exact value of ⌊ln( n )⌋? int(math.log(n)) fails, as math.log(n) might not be accurate enough (e.g. if given 4311231547115195 it outputs 36 but should output 35). I know that ⌊ln( n )⌋ is either ⌊ n.bit_length()-1 ln(2)⌋ or ⌊ n.bit_length() ln(2)⌋. However, in addition to this having the same problem of floating point precision, if the two are unequal I don't know which one to choose. I've also tried computing lower and upper bounds on the value of n.bit_length() ln(2). I tried just using rational approximations of ln(2) given by the harmonic series. However, the alternating harmonic series converges very slowly, and it takes a very long time in some cases for the values to come close enough for me to determine ⌊ n.bit_length() ln(2)⌋ and ⌊ n.bit_length()-1 ln(2)⌋, and I still don't know what to do if they're unequal. I would also appreciate solutions for ⌊ln( n ) 2 ⌋, ⌊ln( n ) 3 ⌋ and ⌊ln( n ) 4 ⌋.
reference_answer: Assuming you only accept integers as input, then the intermediate result (before you floor) can never be an integer value itself. This is because getting an exact integer result means that x must be a power of e (eg. ln(e**2) == 2 ). However, since e is transcendental, none of its integer powers can be rational and therefore cannot be integers. In short, the problem occurs because ln(4311231547115195) == 35.999999999999999947... which is approximately equal to 36 if you lack enough precision to represent that 4. So you just keep increasing the precision, until the intermediate result is not an integer. For instance: def floor_ln(x: int) -> int: if x < 2: if x == 1: return 0 else: raise ValueError(f'positive value required, got: {x}') # use a local context, so we do not alter other system-wide decimal operations with decimal.localcontext() as ctx: # obviously, start with a higher precision for fewer loops (faster execution) ctx.prec = 1 decimal_x = decimal.Decimal(x) while True: res = decimal_x.ln() if res == int(res): # ln(x) has been approximated as an integer, double precision and # try again. Perhaps a better solution might just be to add fixed # amount rather than multiplying by a fixed amount. ctx.prec *= 2 else: return int(res) I'm sure there are better (faster) solutions, where you can compute the appropriate precision to use, rather than just guessing. But it does work for arbitrarily large integers.
llm_attempt: Use the stdlib decimal module instead of float math: Decimal.ln() computes to whatever precision you set. Pick precision comfortably above n's size, e.g. getcontext().prec = n.bit_length() + 20, then L = Decimal(n).ln(); k = int(L) - int() truncates toward zero, which equals floor here since ln(n) >= 0 for n >= 1. Because you control precision directly (unlike float64's fixed ~15-17 digits), you can always add more guard digits, so this doesn't hit the same wall math.log(n) does. Near an integer boundary (L extremely close to an integer), recompute at higher precision and confirm it lands on the same side before trusting it. For floor(ln(n)^2), floor(ln(n)^3), floor(ln(n)^4): compute L once at high precision, then floor(L**2), floor(L**3), floor(L**4) the same way, with the same boundary re-check. mpmath is a solid alternative if you'd rather not manage decimal precision by hand.

question:
Why only creating a task will run the coroutine in python?

There is something I can't understand in this code import asyncio async def fetch_data(param): print(f"Do something with {param}...") await asyncio.sleep(param) print(f"Done with {param}") return f"Result of {param}" async def main(): task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(1)) task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(2)) result2 = await task2 print("Task 2 fully completed") result1 = await task1 print("Task 1 fully completed") return [result1, result2] results = asyncio.run(main()) print(results) The output is Do something with 1... Do something with 2... Done with 1 Done with 2 Task 2 fully completed Task 1 fully completed ['Result of 1', 'Result of 2'] I expected to see Do something with 2... In the first line, but it outputs Do something with 1... first. It seems just creating tasks will run the coroutine, while from what I read and saw, it only registers it in the event loop. The flow should be From results = asyncio.run(main()) the main is registered into event loop Event loop runs the main Two tasks 1,2 are created and registered into the event loop, with status ready By result2 = await task2 , the main is suspended fetch_data(2) is run From this flow, I expect to see Do something with 2... in the first line. Why does this output the Do something with 1...? first? To verify, I run this import asyncio async def fetch_data(param): print(f"Do something with {param}...") await asyncio.sleep(param) print(f"Done with {param}") return f"Result of {param}" async def main(): task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(1)) task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(2)) results = asyncio.r
reference_answer: Let's insert a new line in main following the creation of task2 : import asyncio async def fetch_data(param): print(f"Do something with {param}...") await asyncio.sleep(param) print(f"Done with {param}") return f"Result of {param}" async def main(): task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(1)) task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(2)) print('tasks created') # New statement result2 = await task2 print("Task 2 fully completed") result1 = await task1 print("Task 1 fully completed") return [result1, result2] results = asyncio.run(main()) print(results) The first line of output will be: tasks created By default a call such as asyncio.create_task(fetch_data(1)) creates the task and it can be now scheduled to run -- but it is not automatically started. The current task ( main ) continues to run and any other task that has been created cannot run until main either issues an await statement or completes. Thus, the newly created tasks cannot start running until main issues the call to await task2 . As a result of this await call, other tasks can now run one at a time. Since task1 was created before task2 it is the next task to run. So the task for coro fetch_data(1) will start executing and continue executing until it issues its first await statement. The next task to run will be task2 (coro fetch_data(2) ) since the main task is blocking until task2 completes. Thus the complete output will be: tasks created Do something with 1... Do something with 2... Done with 1 Done with 2 Task 2 fully completed Task 1 fully completed ['Result of 1', 'Result of 2'] Update If you are running Python
llm_attempt: create_task() doesn't just passively 'register' a task - it schedules the coroutine to start running at the very next opportunity the event loop gets, via loop.call_soon(), independent of whether or when anything awaits it. You created task1 then task2, so both are queued to start in that order. When await task2 suspends main and hands control to the loop, the loop drains its ready callbacks FIFO: task1 runs first, printing 'Do something with 1...' and immediately suspending at its own asyncio.sleep(1); then task2 runs, printing 'Do something with 2...' and suspending at sleep(2). Because main is awaiting task2 specifically, it stays suspended until task2 finishes at t=2, by which point task1 already finished at t=1 (its result just sat there done), so await task1 returns instantly right after. The key misconception: awaiting a task controls when you resume, not when the task starts running - it starts as soon as the loop is free to run it.

It's more code than a drop-in fix, but it's the approach most touch-oriented GTK3 apps end up using. If migrating to GTK4 is feasible, its GtkDropDown widget handles touch natively and removes the problem outright instead of working around it.
